Conversation guide

Consent & boundaries

Practice checking in, expressing a limit, and responding when someone wants to slow down or stop. You can change your mind at any point.

Start six-round practiceRead the guide
UnderstandPracticeGet support

A clear check-in gives everyone room to choose. A request to pause or stop should be respected immediately.

Why this topic can feel awkward · Read the guide

A common concern

“How do I say I want to slow down without making things awkward?”

An example of a question you might have.

A boundary can be a complete sentence

You can say what you want, what you do not want, or that you need more time. You do not need a perfect explanation to ask for a pause. If saying it in the moment feels difficult, a calm conversation beforehand can help you find words. Your boundary remains valid even if a partner feels disappointed or expected something different.

Consent is an ongoing conversation

Consent means freely agreeing to a specific activity. A previous yes, an existing relationship, or agreement to one activity does not answer every later question. Ask clearly, listen, and keep checking in. If an answer is uncertain, pause and clarify rather than assuming. When someone says no, asks to stop, or changes their mind, respect that choice without trying to talk them out of it.

Learning context: Berkeley UHS, SHEP, and PATH to Care.

About this story

A six-round story about saying what you want and changing your mind.

You are Morgan, spending an evening with Alex at their apartment. You are both adult college students. You have been kissing, but the pace feels faster than you want. You pull back and take a moment to talk.

Your homepage settings carry over here. Explore six rounds and a few tiny side quests. Change levels, revisit a choice, or pause at any time. No typing required.
